strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect interactive qualitative coding. Its contribution is appropriately framed around evaluating existing systems rather than introducing a new model.

Comparing topic modeling, relational learning, and an LLM-based approach on the same approximately 85,000-tweet corpus provides useful breadth. Holding initial partitions fixed within systems helps comparability, and distinguishing consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness exposes different performance tradeoffs.

The 1,200-pair manual audit, with two judgments per assignment and adjudication, provides valuable evidence beyond embedding metrics. Participant interviews add concrete observations about user control and tool limitations. The appendices disclose prompts, several model settings, and the interview script.
weaknesses: The design does not establish the stated comparison between synchronous and asynchronous collaboration. The introduction defines asynchronous collaboration as independent coding followed by consolidation, but Section 4 evaluates individual codebooks without that consolidation. Comparing three-person teams with individual coders also mixes deliberation with differences in available expertise and effort. Participant allocation, reuse across the 27 participation slots filled by 20 researchers, session duration, and annotation effort are insufficiently documented.

The statistical evidence for collaboration effects is not convincing. Each system has only two synchronous groups and three individual runs, yielding one synchronous codebook pair and three overlapping asynchronous pairs. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without specifying their sampling units or accounting for dependence within sessions and shared codebooks. Treating themes or matches as independent observations would overstate the effective sample size. Exact p-values, session-level uncertainty, and multiple-comparison handling are absent; 'near statistically significant' results should remain inconclusive.

Correctness is insufficiently defined and inconsistently interpreted. Section 5 describes checking predicted document–theme assignments, but Figure 4 reports F1 without explaining recall, negative cases, or averaging. Its cumulative quartile labels also differ from the text's description of per-quartile results. The claim that asynchronous topic modeling produces more accurate assignments is supported only at the first plotted threshold; synchronous performance is higher at the next two, and both tie overall. Uncertainty and treatment of the 0.7–16.1% invalid-label outputs in Table 4 are unclear.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger construct validation. Maximum-over-theme matching is sensitive to codebook size, yet final theme counts, size distributions, and precise matching rules are missing. Centroid similarities cluster around 0.94–0.98 despite substantially lower document overlap, raising questions about discriminative value. The manual correctness audit does not establish that these consistency and cohesion metrics track researchers' judgments of thematic quality. Calibration against human judgments or suitable null comparisons would strengthen the framework.

Several conclusions exceed the experimental scope. Richer interaction may explain the relational system's apparent benefit from synchronous work, but interface, supervision, and underlying model vary together, so that mechanism is not isolated. Likewise, results from Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct with one inference setup cannot establish broad limitations of LLM-assisted coding or its scalability. These claims should be restricted to the tested configurations unless supported by additional comparisons.

The interview evidence is exploratory rather than a rigorous comparative user study. Appendix C acknowledges that some interviews were omitted but provides no completed sample counts by condition. Individual and group interviews also differ systematically, and the analysis procedure is unspecified. These omissions weaken claims about differences in perceived agency, difficulty, and tool inadequacy between conditions.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix material. Missing details include the exact embedding checkpoint, final codebooks, selected prompt per session, prompt-selection sample size, generation settings, correctness rubric, and statistical aggregation procedure. Artifacts are promised without an access link. The study offers promising descriptive observations, but the design, inference, and reporting issues require revision before it supports a sound Findings recommendation.
